title: Wasp: Efficient Asynchronous Single-Source Shortest Path on Multicore Systems via Work Stealing
problem: State-of-the-art parallel SSSP algorithms (Δ-stepping) create parallelism through priority coarsening, inducing redundant computations that limit scalability and parallel efficiency on modern multicore systems.
motivation: SSSP is fundamental in many applications (routing, social networks, graph analytics). Existing algorithms waste parallelism through coarse-grained priority queues, limiting speedups on multicore CPUs.
method: Wasp computes shortest paths (fastest routes from one starting point to all others) on multiple processor cores using work stealing—when one thread runs out of tasks, it borrows work from a busier thread. Unlike older methods like Δ-stepping that create redundant computations upfront, Wasp only produces redundancy when threads actually need more work. Threads operate asynchronously (without waiting for synchronization), which handles the irregular work patterns that shortest-path algorithms naturally create.
key_novelty: Using priority-aware work stealing (where idle threads take high-priority tasks from busy ones), Wasp ensures redundant computation in shortest-path algorithms only occurs when threads need more work, not by design upfront.
contributions: Wasp SSSP algorithm with priority-aware work stealing
Efficient priority queue management via stealing on demand
Geometric mean speedup 2.23x on AMD Zen 3 and 2.16x on Intel Sapphire Rapids (128 threads)

metrics.comparison: Competitive or better vs. GAP, GBBS, MultiQueues, Galois, Δ*-stepping, ρ-stepping

limitations: CPU-only focus; 13 graphs may not cover all real-world sizes/topologies; comparison on specific hardware platforms
primary_theme: Efficient Parallel SSSP via Priority-Aware Work Stealing
